title: Binary search trees
summary: Use a binary search tree to choose a left or right branch. Find one target, handle a missing value, and learn why the tree shape matters.
introduction: A guessing game becomes easier when someone says smaller or bigger. A binary search tree stores values so each comparison tells us which branch can still contain the answer.
learningObjectives: Explain the smaller-left and larger-right rule
Trace a search that skips an unneeded branch
Describe how tree height changes search work

blocks.text: A **binary search tree**, or BST, is a binary tree with an ordering rule. In this lesson, every value in a node's left branch is smaller, and every value in its right branch is larger.
The rule applies to whole branches, not just the two children. The same rule must hold at every node. We use distinct values here, so there are no duplicates to place.
For a search, compare the target with the current value. Equal means found. Smaller means try the left branch. Larger means try the right branch. The other branch can be skipped.

items: Build root 8, left child 3, and right child 10.
Search for 10. Compare it with 8; 10 is larger.
Move to the right child. Its value is 10, so the target is found.
Print 10. We never needed to inspect node 3.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

Use a separate local C++17 compiler. Save this complete program as main.cpp; see Language setup.

variants.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

root = Node(8, Node(3), Node(10))
current = root
target = 10
found = -1
while current is not None:
    if target == current.value:
        found = current.value
        break
    current = current.left if target < current.value else current.right
print(found)

blocks.text: The loop follows just one branch at each step. An empty link ends an unsuccessful search. We use -1 to mean missing only because all values in this tiny example are non-negative. A reusable function should return a separate found flag or an optional result.
Check the small and tricky cases
An empty tree immediately gives missing. Searching for the root succeeds in one comparison. Searching for 6 goes left to 3, then right to an empty link and gives -1.

A **balanced** tree keeps its height small. Search can then take O(log n) work, read O of log n. Roughly, doubling the item count adds only one more level to a neatly balanced tree. An ordinary BST does not balance itself: inserting 1, 2, 3, and 4 in order can make a long one-sided chain. Search then takes O(n) worst-case work.
Before adding duplicate values, choose a rule: reject them, count them in a node, or place them consistently with a matching search rule. The strict smaller/larger rule here excludes duplicates.

items: The output becomes -1. Trace 8, then 3, then the empty right branch. Missing is a useful result, not a failed loop.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not assume that every binary tree is a binary search tree. Branch skipping is correct only while the ordering rule holds everywhere.
